cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C>0 such that for every integer m≥1, every family S⊆2^{[m]}, every weight vector w∈ℝ≥0^m and every 0<ε<1, there is a reweighting w̃∈ℝ≥0^m with at most C·CL(S)/ε² nonzero coordinates and satisfying (1−ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ≤∑_{i∈A}w̃ᵢ≤(1+ε)∑_{i∈A}wᵢ simultaneously for every A∈S?
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.
cards.status_note: Published definitions, main bound and Conjecture 23 checked through 11 September 2026, together with the related May 2026 report and subsequent searches. No matching logarithm-free universal bound or counterexample was located.

progress.text: The ICALP paper proves a universe-size-independent bound with logarithmic overhead and poses the O(CL(S)/ε²) bound as Conjecture 23.
A related CSP sparsification report still states its broad characterizations with polylogarithmic and accuracy factors; its abstract does not settle the sharper conjecture.

importance.reason: A general multiplicative sparsification conjecture linking support size to a structural invariant, with consequences for cuts, codes and CSPs. The existing numerical score is retained during formulation review.

sentences: A sparsifier retains and reweights a few coordinates while approximately preserving every set’s total weight.
The conjecture asks for a support bound proportional to chain length divided by ε².
Chain length is measured through the union-closure, so even an incomparable collection of singleton sets can have large chain length.
The published upper bound has extra logarithmic factors, which are precisely the remaining loss in the question.
A resolution would establish whether this structural parameter completely controls multiplicative sparsification up to a universal constant.

references.title: Multiplicative Error Set System Sparsification: A Simpler Proof via Chain Length Contraction
references.authors: Brakensiek, Joshua; Guruswami, Venkatesan; Putterman, Aaron

cards.definitions: Here [m]={1,…,m}, and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is {i:w̃ᵢ>0}; coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as ∑wᵢ=1 is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length ℓ consists of distinct coordinates a₁,…,a_ℓ and distinct sets A₁,…,A_ℓ∈S with aᵢ∈Aᵢ for every i and aⱼ∉Aᵢ whenever i<j. CL(S) is the maximum possible ℓ, allowing ℓ=0. Equivalently, take the union-closure U(S)={⋃T:T⊆S}, including the empty union; CL(S) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from ∅ in U(S). Thus CL(S)=0 when S is empty or contains only ∅. It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A (1±ε) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and ε. The source allows ε>0; values ε≥1 admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to 0<ε<1 preserves it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than C·CL(S)/ε² coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.

context_blocks.title: Preserve all set weights with fewer coordinates
context_blocks.text: A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

context_blocks.title: One set can be represented by one weighted coordinate
context_blocks.text: If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

context_blocks.title: Union-closure sees constraints absent from direct containment
context_blocks.text: If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so CL(S)=m. With unit original weights and ε<1, every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

context_blocks.title: The current upper bound still has logarithmic overhead
context_blocks.text: The paper gives support O(CL(S)·log²(CL(S)/ε)·(log log(CL(S)/ε))²/ε²), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

context_blocks.title: Existence and computation remain separate
context_blocks.text: The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.

cards.context:
A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so CL(S)=m. With unit original weights and ε<1, every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

The paper gives support O(CL(S)·log²(CL(S)/ε)·(log log(CL(S)/ε))²/ε²), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
